unit.name: Paper 2: Judaism
unit.subtitle: Beliefs and practices of Judaism as the second religion

lessons.title: The Nature of God, Shekhinah and the Messiah
lessons.description: The Almighty as One, Creator, Law-Giver and Judge; the Shekhinah; and Jewish beliefs about the Messiah.
lessons.content_html:
The Nature of the Almighty

The Edexcel spec uses the title ‘the Almighty’ as the formal name for God in Judaism. Jewish belief is centred on the absolute oneness of the Almighty — monotheism is foundational. The Almighty is One: not one of many gods, not a God with parts or persons, but the absolutely singular source and sustainer of all existence. This is stated in the Shema (Deuteronomy 6:4): “Hear, O Israel: the Lord our God, the Lord is one.”

Genesis 2 is the named source for several of the Almighty’s key characteristics:

Creator: The Almighty is the Creator of all existence, bringing the universe into being from nothing (creation ex nihilo). Genesis 2 describes the Almighty forming man from the dust of the ground and breathing life into him — humanity has a special, intimate relationship with the Creator. Jews today see creation as a gift requiring responsible stewardship.

Law-Giver: The Almighty is the source of all moral and religious law. The Torah (especially the Ten Commandments in Exodus 20) represents the Almighty’s revealed law. Living according to the Almighty’s law is not merely a religious duty but the means by which Jewish individuals and communities reflect the divine will in everyday life.

Judge: The Almighty holds all humanity accountable for their actions. Jewish theology teaches that the Almighty sees all deeds, knows all intentions, and will judge righteously. This belief in divine justice motivates ethical living — if the Almighty judges, then moral behaviour ultimately matters.

Key Fact

The four Edexcel-named characteristics of the Almighty: One (absolute monotheism — Shema, Deuteronomy 6:4), Creator (Genesis 2), Law-Giver (Torah, Exodus 20), Judge (holds all humanity accountable). These characteristics are tested in 3-mark and 4-mark questions.

The Shekhinah

Shekhinah means ‘divine dwelling’ — the presence of the Almighty among the Jewish people. The named anchor text is 2 Chronicles 7:1–3, which describes the Shekhinah descending as a cloud and filling the Temple when Solomon dedicated it: “When Solomon had finished praying, fire came down from heaven and consumed the burnt offering… and the glory of the Lord filled the temple.” The priests could not enter because of the overwhelming divine presence.

The Shekhinah is both comforting and awesome. Jewish theology developed the concept to express how the transcendent, infinite Almighty can be encountered in human experience — in the Temple, in the synagogue, in the home, and wherever Jews gather to pray. For many Jews, the Shekhinah is also associated with the feminine aspect of the divine.

Orthodox Judaism maintains that the Shekhinah was uniquely present in the Temple and that its absence today (since the Temple’s destruction in 70 CE) is a mark of divine distance pending the Messianic age and the rebuilding of the Temple. The Shekhinah will return fully when the Messiah comes. Reform Judaism tends to understand the Shekhinah as God’s presence available in every genuine moment of prayer, community and ethical action — not waiting for a physical Temple. This makes the concept more immediately accessible but less tied to specific historical events.

The Messiah and the Messianic Age

Messiah comes from the Hebrew mashiach (‘anointed one’). In Judaism the Messiah is a future human king — not divine — from the lineage of King David who will redeem the Jewish people and bring a universal age of peace. The named anchor text is Jeremiah 23:5–8, which describes the Almighty promising to raise a righteous Branch from David’s line who will reign wisely and bring justice: “The days are coming… when I will raise up for David a righteous Branch, a King who will reign wisely and do what is just and right in the land.”

The messianic age will involve: the ingathering of exiled Jews to Israel; the rebuilding of the Temple in Jerusalem; universal recognition of the Almighty; the end of war and injustice. Jews believe the Messianic age has not yet arrived — the world still contains war, injustice and suffering.

Key Fact

Orthodox Jews believe in a personal Messiah — a specific future individual from David’s line — who will physically rebuild the Temple and redeem the Jewish people. Reform Jews tend to reinterpret this as the ‘messianic age’: a future era of universal justice brought about through human effort and moral progress, without necessarily involving a specific individual. Jeremiah 23:5–8 is the named source for messianic hope.

Both Orthodox and Reform Judaism place responsibility on the Jewish people to actively work toward the conditions of the messianic age. Tikkun olam (‘repair of the world’) is the Jewish ethical concept that every act of justice, charity, compassion and righteousness contributes to repairing the broken world and hastening the time of redemption. This means the messianic hope is not passive waiting but active ethical engagement. A 12-mark Discuss answer on this topic should develop this active dimension alongside any divergence between Orthodox and Reform positions.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For the 5-mark ‘Explain two with sources’ question, use 2 Chronicles 7:1–3 (for the Shekhinah) or Jeremiah 23:5–8 (for the Messiah) as your named sources. Note the exact chapter and verse — examiners award the 5th mark only for a clearly identifiable, named source. For the 12-mark Discuss question on the Messiah, the Orthodox/Reform divergence is essential: develop both positions with equal depth. The most common student error is treating the Messiah as divine in Judaism — the Jewish Messiah is a human king, not a divine saviour in the Christian sense. SPaG rewards correct spelling of ‘Shekhinah’, ‘messianic’ and ‘monotheism’.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The Almighty has four Edexcel-named characteristics: One (absolute monotheism), Creator (Genesis 2), Law-Giver and Judge. These shape how Jews understand their relationship with God in daily life.
  • The Shekhinah is the divine presence dwelling among the Jewish people, dramatically described in 2 Chronicles 7:1–3. Orthodox Jews associate it with the Temple; Reform Jews see it as present wherever Jews pray and act ethically.
  • The Messiah (from David’s line, Jeremiah 23:5–8) will inaugurate the messianic age of universal peace. Orthodox Jews expect a specific future individual; Reform Jews emphasise the messianic age brought by human ethical effort.

practice_questions.text: Outline three characteristics of the Almighty in Judaism.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for three characteristics with a brief explanation. Acceptable: One (absolute monotheism — the Almighty is the singular source of all existence, as stated in the Shema); Creator (brought all existence into being from nothing, forming humanity intimately as in Genesis 2); Law-Giver (source of all moral and religious law, including the Torah); Judge (holds all humanity accountable for their actions, motivating ethical living).

practice_questions.text: Describe the Jewish teaching about the Shekhinah.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 3 marks. Shekhinah means 'divine dwelling' or 'divine presence' (1 mark). 2 Chronicles 7:1-3 describes it descending as a cloud filling Solomon's Temple at its dedication (1 mark). It expresses how the transcendent Almighty can be encountered in human experience — in the Temple, synagogue, home and prayer (1 mark).

practice_questions.text: Explain two Jewish beliefs about the Messiah.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks per belief. Belief 1: the Messiah will be a human king from the line of King David who will restore Jewish sovereignty and rebuild the Temple — he is not divine but a specially anointed human leader; this belief reflects continued trust in the Almighty's promises. Belief 2: divergent understandings of the Messiah — Orthodox Jews expect a specific future individual who will physically rebuild the Temple; Reform Jews reinterpret this as the 'messianic age' of universal justice brought by human moral effort.

practice_questions.text:
Explain two ways in which belief in the Almighty as Creator shapes Jewish life today.
In your answer, include a reference to a source of wisdom and authority.
practice_questions.marks: 2 + 2 marks + 1 for named source. Way 1: belief in the Almighty as Creator motivates environmental responsibility — creation is a gift from the Creator and Jews have a duty to protect it; this connects to Shabbat observance (rest for creation, not just humans). Way 2: belief that humanity is formed by the Almighty in an intimate act (Genesis 2 — the Almighty breathed life into Adam) gives every human being inherent dignity and worth, motivating justice and care for others. 5th mark: ‘Genesis 2 describes the Almighty forming man from dust and breathing life into him, showing the intimate relationship between Creator and creation.’

practice_questions.text:
'Belief in the Messiah is the most important belief in Judaism.'
Discuss this statement.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (10-12): Both sides developed with named sources; justified conclusion. Arguments in support: Messianic hope gives Jews a future-oriented purpose and ethical motivation (tikkun olam); Jeremiah 23:5-8 anchors this in authoritative scripture; the hope for justice and universal peace is central to Jewish prayer (the Amidah includes prayers for the Messiah's coming); without this hope Judaism would lack its eschatological horizon. Arguments against: the Shema's declaration of monotheism (Deuteronomy 6:4 — 'Hear O Israel, the Lord our God, the Lord is one') is the most foundational affirmation in Judaism — recited twice daily, at deathbeds; keeping the Mitzvot (commandments) is the most practical and immediate expression of Jewish faith; the covenant relationship with the Almighty (Genesis 17, Exodus 20) is prior to any messianic belief. Secure (7-9): Both sides; at least Jeremiah 23:5-8 named. Developing (4-6): One-sided. Emerging (1-3): Brief.

practice_questions.text: Explain two differences between Orthodox and Reform Jewish beliefs about the Messiah.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks per difference. Difference 1: Orthodox Jews believe in a personal Messiah — a specific future individual from David's line who will physically rebuild the Temple; Reform Jews tend to understand the messianic hope as a collective future era (the messianic age) rather than one specific person. Difference 2: Orthodox Jews see the coming of the Messiah as a miraculous divine act; many Reform Jews emphasise human moral effort (tikkun olam) as bringing about the conditions of justice and peace associated with the messianic age.

lessons.title: The Covenant and Jewish Moral Principles
lessons.description: The Abrahamic and Sinai covenants, Pikuach Nefesh, the Mitzvot, and Jewish beliefs about life after death.
lessons.content_html:
The Covenant with Abraham

The relationship between the Jewish people and the Almighty is fundamentally one of covenant. The first great covenant is the Abrahamic covenant, recorded in Genesis 17. The Almighty promised Abraham: a great nation of descendants; the land of Canaan (the Promised Land); and a special ongoing relationship between the Almighty and Abraham’s descendants. In return, Abraham and his male descendants were to observe circumcision as a physical sign of the covenant in every generation.

This covenant is unconditional in one sense — the Almighty’s promise to Abraham’s descendants stands regardless of their behaviour. But it is also relational: the Jewish people are called to live faithfully in response to the Almighty’s faithfulness. The Promised Land is both a concrete historical reality and a symbol of the relationship between the Almighty and the Jewish people.

The Sinai Covenant and the Ten Commandments

The second great covenant is the Sinai Covenant, recorded in Exodus 20. Through Moses, the Almighty gave the Jewish people the Decalogue (Ten Commandments). The Decalogue establishes both duties to the Almighty (no other gods, no idols, no misuse of the divine name, observe Shabbat, honour parents) and duties to fellow human beings (no murder, adultery, theft, false testimony or coveting).

Key Fact

Two key covenants: the Abrahamic covenant (Genesis 17 — land, descendants, relationship; sign = circumcision) and the Sinai Covenant (Exodus 20 — the Ten Commandments / Decalogue as the terms of the Jewish people’s relationship with the Almighty). Both are the foundation of Jewish identity and practice.

Sanctity of Life and Pikuach Nefesh

Jewish ethics places an exceptionally high value on human life. Sanctity of life means that every human life has infinite worth because it is created by the Almighty in His image. This principle leads directly to Pikuach Nefesh — the principle that preserving life (nefesh = soul/life) overrides nearly all other commandments.

The named anchor text is Talmud Yoma 83–84, which states that Shabbat laws may be broken to save a life: “If a person sees a child who has fallen into a well, he may break the Shabbat to save it.” In practice, Pikuach Nefesh means that a Jewish doctor can and must work on Shabbat to save a patient; a pregnant woman is not required to fast on Yom Kippur if it endangers her health.

Orthodox Judaism applies Pikuach Nefesh strictly and carefully — it suspends specific commandments only when there is a genuine, immediate threat to life. The principle does not override every inconvenience; Orthodox rabbis consider cases individually. Reform Judaism applies the principle more broadly: if keeping a commandment causes significant harm or suffering, Reform Jews may view this as a Pikuach Nefesh consideration. For example, Reform Jews are more likely to apply Pikuach Nefesh to mental health as well as physical health, which has implications for topics like fasting and end-of-life care.

The Mitzvot and Free Will

The Mitzvot (singular: mitzvah) are the 613 commandments in the Torah. They cover every aspect of Jewish life — worship, food, business, family relationships, charity and social justice. The named source is Mishneh Torah by Maimonides — specifically the Sefer Madda (Book of Knowledge), which establishes the philosophical foundations of the Mitzvot.

Crucially, the Mitzvot are observed through free will. The Almighty does not compel obedience. Humans have the capacity to choose righteousness or sin, and this makes obedience meaningful and disobedience culpable. Maimonides emphasises that the Almighty’s knowledge of future human choices does not remove human freedom — this is one of the deepest puzzles in Jewish theology.

Jewish Beliefs about Life after Death

Jewish beliefs about life after death are notably less defined than in Christianity or Islam. The Torah’s focus is primarily on living ethically in this world. The named source is Ecclesiastes 12, which reflects on the nature of human mortality and uses somewhat ambiguous language about the spirit returning to the Almighty who gave it. This ambiguity reflects the diversity of views within Judaism.

Key Fact

Orthodox Judaism affirms bodily resurrection (techiyat ha-meitim) as a key belief — the dead will be resurrected in the Messianic age. Orthodox Jews also believe in the World to Come (Olam Ha-Ba) and sometimes Gehinnom (a place of purification). Reform Judaism tends to de-emphasise physical resurrection, focusing instead on the spiritual legacy of how one lived. Ecclesiastes 12 (the spirit returns to the Almighty) is the named anchor source.

Key contrasts: Orthodox Judaism believes in resurrection of the body in the Messianic age; Christianity teaches resurrection through Christ as demonstrated in the resurrection of Jesus (John 11:25 — ‘I am the resurrection and the life’). Judaism does not have a highly developed doctrine of heaven and hell; Christianity has more defined teaching on these (John 3:16 on eternal life; the Catholic doctrine of purgatory). Both traditions see ethical living now as shaping what comes after death. Jewish afterlife belief is tied to collective redemption in the Messianic age; Christian afterlife is individual resurrection and judgment.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For the 5-mark question, name either Genesis 17 (Abrahamic covenant), Exodus 20 (Sinai Covenant / Decalogue), Talmud Yoma 83–84 (Pikuach Nefesh) or Ecclesiastes 12 (afterlife). These are your Edexcel-named sources — naming any one earns the 5th mark. Do not write ‘the Talmud says’ without naming the tractate. For the 12-mark Discuss question on the afterlife (1.8*), develop both the Jewish and Christian sides with named sources: Ecclesiastes 12 for Judaism, John 11:25 for Christianity. The most common error is treating Jewish afterlife beliefs as simply ‘no afterlife’ — Orthodox Judaism has detailed beliefs about resurrection and Olam Ha-Ba. SPaG rewards correct spelling of ‘Pikuach Nefesh’, ‘Mitzvot’ and ‘Maimonides’.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Two covenants shape Jewish identity: the Abrahamic covenant (Genesis 17 — land, descendants, circumcision) and the Sinai Covenant (Exodus 20 — Decalogue / Ten Commandments through Moses).
  • Pikuach Nefesh (Talmud Yoma 83–84) means preserving life overrides almost all other commandments. The 613 Mitzvot (Maimonides’ Mishneh Torah Sefer Madda) are observed through free will, making obedience morally meaningful.
  • Jewish afterlife beliefs are varied: Orthodox affirms resurrection and Olam Ha-Ba; Reform focuses on spiritual legacy. Ecclesiastes 12 is the named source. This is the 1.8* comparison point requiring contrast with Christian resurrection beliefs.

practice_questions.text: Outline three features of the covenant between the Almighty and Abraham (Genesis 17).
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for three features. Acceptable: the Almighty promised Abraham a great nation of descendants; the Almighty promised the land of Canaan (the Promised Land) to Abraham's descendants; circumcision was established as the physical sign of the covenant; the Almighty established a special ongoing relationship with Abraham's descendants; the covenant was renewed with Isaac and Jacob.

practice_questions.text: Describe the principle of Pikuach Nefesh in Judaism.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 3 marks. Pikuach Nefesh means preserving life takes precedence over almost all commandments (1 mark). The Talmud Yoma 83-84 teaches that Shabbat may be broken to save a life (1 mark). In practice: a doctor may work on Shabbat; a pregnant woman need not fast on Yom Kippur if it endangers health (1 mark for application).

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which the Mitzvot shape the daily life of Jewish people today.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks per way. Way 1: kashrut (food laws as part of the Mitzvot) shapes what a Jew eats at every meal, requiring separate utensils for meat and dairy, avoiding non-kosher foods; this daily discipline creates a constant reminder of the covenant and Jewish identity. Way 2: Shabbat observance (commanded in the Decalogue at Exodus 20) shapes one day every week — from sunset Friday to nightfall Saturday, work is forbidden; families gather, synagogue is attended, and the rhythm of holy time structures the week.

practice_questions.text:
Explain two Jewish teachings about life after death.
In your answer, include a reference to a source of wisdom and authority.
practice_questions.marks: 2 + 2 marks + 1 for named source. Teaching 1: Orthodox Judaism teaches bodily resurrection (techiyat ha-meitim) — the dead will be raised in the Messianic age; this is tied to the collective redemption of the Jewish people. Teaching 2: Reform Judaism tends to emphasise the spiritual legacy of how one lived rather than physical resurrection — the focus is on living ethically now; some Reform Jews believe in the soul's return to the Almighty. 5th mark: ‘Ecclesiastes 12 reflects on human mortality and states that the spirit returns to the Almighty who gave it.’

practice_questions.text:
'Jewish beliefs about life after death are less important than Christian beliefs.'
Discuss this statement.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (10-12): Both sides developed with named sources; justified conclusion. Arguments in support: Jewish scripture (Torah) focuses primarily on this life and ethical behaviour rather than the afterlife; Jewish practice centres on covenant, commandments and tikkun olam in the present; the ambiguity of Ecclesiastes 12 suggests afterlife is not a central doctrinal concern; some Jewish thinkers argue that excessive focus on afterlife rewards distorts moral motivation. Arguments against: Orthodox Judaism has detailed and important beliefs about resurrection, Olam Ha-Ba and Gehinnom; the messianic hope (Jeremiah 23:5-8) includes collective eschatology; Christian afterlife beliefs (John 11:25 — resurrection; John 3:16 — eternal life) are explicitly tied to faith in Christ — one tradition's afterlife emphasis does not automatically make another's less important; many Orthodox Jews see resurrection as central to Jewish faith. Secure (7-9): Both sides; at least Ecclesiastes 12 or John 11:25 named. Developing (4-6): One-sided. Emerging (1-3): Brief.

practice_questions.text: Explain two reasons why Maimonides' Mishneh Torah is important in Judaism.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks per reason. Reason 1: the Mishneh Torah systematised all 613 Mitzvot for the first time in a single, comprehensive, accessible code — it made the vast body of Jewish law navigable for ordinary Jews; the Sefer Madda established the philosophical foundations of why Jews observe the Mitzvot. Reason 2: Maimonides (1138-1204 CE) was the foremost legal and philosophical authority of medieval Judaism — his 13 Principles of Faith (also in the Mishneh Torah) became widely accepted as a summary of core Jewish belief, showing that the Mishneh Torah shaped not just legal but also theological understanding.

lessons.title: Jewish Worship: Synagogue, Prayer and Sacred Texts
lessons.description: Public worship, the Tenakh and Talmud, kashrut, private prayer, and the Shema and Amidah.
lessons.content_html:
Jewish Public Worship

Jewish public worship takes place primarily in the synagogue. Psalm 116:12–19 asks “How can I repay the Lord for all his goodness to me?” — capturing the spirit of gratitude and obligation that motivates Jewish communal worship. Services in the synagogue involve prayer, readings from the Torah and Haftarah (Prophets), and a rabbi’s sermon. Communal prayer requires a minyan — a quorum of ten adult Jews (Orthodox Judaism requires ten adult males; Reform Judaism counts women equally).

The Tenakh and Talmud

The Tenakh is the Hebrew Bible — an acronym from Torah (Five Books: Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, Deuteronomy), Nevi’im (Prophets) and Ketuvim (Writings). The Torah is the most sacred section, believed by Orthodox Jews to have been revealed directly by the Almighty to Moses at Sinai.

The Talmud is the compilation of rabbinic wisdom — the Mishnah (the oral law codified) plus the Gemara (rabbinic commentary). Perkei Avot 2 (from the Talmud) teaches that a Torah scholar should ensure all their work has a foundation in Torah study — illustrating how the Talmud extends Tenakh into practical ethical guidance for daily life.

Key Fact

The Tenakh = Torah + Nevi’im + Ketuvim. The Talmud = Mishnah (oral law codified ~200 CE) + Gemara (rabbinic commentary). The named source Perkei Avot 2 is from the Mishnah, offering practical ethical wisdom. Orthodox Jews regard both the written Torah and the oral Torah (Talmud) as divinely given; Reform Jews see the Talmud as authoritative tradition open to reinterpretation.

Food Laws: Kashrut

Kashrut is the system of Jewish food laws. Kosher means ‘fit’ — food that may be eaten. Treifah (‘torn’) means forbidden food. The named source is Deuteronomy 14:3–10, which lists forbidden animals (e.g. pigs, shellfish) and permitted ones (e.g. animals that chew their cud and have split hooves, such as cattle). A key rule is the separation of meat and dairy — derived from the command “Do not boil a young goat in its mother’s milk” (Exodus 23:19). Many kosher homes have separate sets of crockery and utensils for meat and dairy.

Orthodox Jews observe kashrut strictly in and out of the home. Reform Jews may observe kashrut as a matter of Jewish identity and tradition, but many do so selectively, seeing the laws as culturally significant rather than divinely commanded in every detail.

Private Prayer

Jews pray three times a day — morning (Shacharit), afternoon (Mincha) and evening (Maariv) — whether in synagogue or privately at home. Psalm 55:16–23 describes calling on the Almighty evening, morning and noon — the biblical basis for three daily prayers. Private prayer can be in any language and does not require a minyan.

The Shema and the Amidah

The Shema is the central statement of Jewish faith, from Deuteronomy 6:4: “Hear, O Israel: the Lord our God, the Lord is one.” It is recited morning and evening, during certain synagogue services, and at the moment of death. It affirms the absolute oneness of the Almighty. The Mezuzah — a small case fixed to the doorpost of Jewish homes containing the Shema passage — is a constant physical reminder of the covenant obligation.

Key Fact

The Shema (Deuteronomy 6:4) is the defining statement of Jewish monotheism: “Hear, O Israel: the Lord our God, the Lord is one.” It is recited at least twice daily. The Mezuzah on the doorpost keeps this affirmation present in everyday life. The Amidah (Standing Prayer) is the primary structured prayer of Jewish worship.

The Amidah (Standing Prayer) is the central prayer of every Jewish service. It consists of nineteen blessings (originally eighteen, hence the alternative name Shemoneh Esreh) covering praise of the Almighty, petitions for personal and communal needs, and thanksgiving. It is recited standing, in silence, facing Jerusalem (reflecting the temple’s direction and the Almighty’s presence). Orthodox Jews recite the Amidah in its traditional Hebrew text; Reform communities often use abridged or translated versions. The combination of the Shema (declaration of faith) and the Amidah (prayer of petition and praise) forms the backbone of daily Jewish worship.

The 2.4* comparison point: Jewish prayer (Shema, Amidah) and Christian prayer (Lord’s Prayer, Matthew 6:9–13). Key parallels: both involve set and personal prayers; both include praise, petition and thanksgiving; both are addressed to a personal God. Key differences: Jewish prayer is structured around the Mitzvot — reciting the Shema is itself a commandment; Christian prayer is primarily relational. Jews pray facing Jerusalem; Christians typically pray toward the altar or have no fixed direction. The Amidah is recited three times daily as an obligation; Christian prayer frequency varies by tradition.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For the 5-mark question, named sources include Psalm 116:12–19 (communal worship), Perkei Avot 2 (Tenakh/Talmud), Deuteronomy 14:3–10 (kashrut), Psalm 55:16–23 (three daily prayers) and Deuteronomy 6:4 (the Shema and Mezuzah). Name the specific book, chapter and verse. For the 12-mark Discuss question on the Shema or worship (2.4*), develop the Christian comparison — use the Lord’s Prayer (Matthew 6:9–13) as your Christian named source. The most common error is treating kashrut as merely cultural preference — for Orthodox Jews it is a divine commandment derived from Deuteronomy 14:3–10. SPaG rewards correct spelling of ‘kashrut’, ‘kosher’, ‘Mezuzah’ and ‘Amidah’.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The Tenakh (Torah + Nevi’im + Ketuvim) and the Talmud (Mishnah + Gemara, including Perkei Avot 2) are the foundation of Jewish religious authority. Kashrut (Deuteronomy 14:3–10) governs what Jews eat; separation of meat and dairy is a key practice.
  • Private prayer is practised three times daily (Psalm 55:16–23). The Shema (Deuteronomy 6:4) is the central declaration of Jewish monotheism, recited twice daily and physically present in the Mezuzah on doorposts.
  • The Amidah (Standing Prayer) of nineteen blessings is the core of every Jewish service, recited standing and facing Jerusalem. Together the Shema and Amidah form the backbone of daily Jewish worship — this is the 2.4* comparison-marked spec point.

practice_questions.text: Outline three features of Jewish public worship in the synagogue.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for three features. Acceptable: Torah readings and Haftarah (Prophets) readings; recitation of the Shema; the Amidah (Standing Prayer) recited by the congregation; a rabbi's sermon; communal minyan (quorum of ten); singing of hymns and psalms; prayers facing Jerusalem.

practice_questions.text: Describe the Jewish food laws (kashrut).
practice_questions.marks: Up to 3 marks. Kashrut divides food into kosher (permitted) and treifah (forbidden) (1 mark). Deuteronomy 14:3-10 lists forbidden animals including pigs and shellfish; permitted animals chew the cud and have split hooves (1 mark). The separation of meat and dairy is required — many kosher homes have separate utensils for each (1 mark).

practice_questions.text: Explain two reasons why the Shema is important for Jewish people today.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks per reason. Reason 1: the Shema (Deuteronomy 6:4 — 'Hear O Israel, the Lord our God, the Lord is one') is the foundational declaration of Jewish monotheism — reciting it twice daily keeps the belief in God's absolute oneness at the centre of daily life. Reason 2: the Shema is recited at the moment of death — making it both the daily affirmation and the final statement of faith; this gives it unique significance as a whole-life practice expressing the Jew's ultimate allegiance to the Almighty.

practice_questions.text:
Explain two ways in which Jewish sacred texts shape the lives of Jewish people today.
In your answer, include a reference to a source of wisdom and authority.
practice_questions.marks: 2 + 2 marks + 1 for named source. Way 1: the Torah (part of the Tenakh) provides the 613 Mitzvot including kashrut and Shabbat that structure everyday life; Torah readings in synagogue every Shabbat and Monday/Thursday keep the text continuously present. Way 2: the Talmud (especially texts like Perkei Avot 2) provides practical ethical guidance for everyday situations that the Torah's broad principles do not directly address; it has shaped how Jews apply the Mitzvot in changing historical contexts. 5th mark: ‘Perkei Avot 2 teaches that all work should be done with Torah as its foundation.’

practice_questions.text:
'The Shema is more important than the Amidah in Jewish worship.'
Discuss this statement.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (10-12): Both sides developed with named sources; justified conclusion. Arguments in support: the Shema (Deuteronomy 6:4) is the most fundamental declaration of Jewish monotheism and the defining statement of Jewish faith; it is recited at the critical moments of life and death; the Mezuzah ensures it is physically present in every Jewish home; it is the first prayer taught to Jewish children. Arguments against: the Amidah (nineteen blessings) is the central prayer of every Jewish service — it is obligatory at every shacharit, mincha and maariv; it covers praise, petition and thanksgiving in a comprehensive way; some rabbinic opinion holds that the Amidah is the most important prayer because it constitutes the formal 'service of the heart'; both are essential and the comparison is partly artificial. Secure (7-9): Both sides; Deuteronomy 6:4 named. Developing (4-6): One-sided. Emerging (1-3): Brief.

practice_questions.text: Explain two differences between Orthodox and Reform Jewish approaches to kashrut.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks per difference. Difference 1: Orthodox Jews regard kashrut as a divine commandment derived directly from Deuteronomy 14:3-10 and the Talmud — they observe it strictly at home and outside, including only eating in certified kosher establishments; Reform Jews may observe kashrut selectively as a matter of Jewish identity rather than divine obligation. Difference 2: Orthodox Jews maintain strict separation of meat and dairy (separate utensils, pots, waiting periods between eating meat and dairy); many Reform Jews observe this only partially or not at all, since they see the Oral Torah as tradition open to re-evaluation rather than divinely binding law.

lessons.title: Family Life, Shabbat, Festivals and the Synagogue
lessons.description: Jewish life-cycle rituals, Shabbat, major festivals and the features of the synagogue.
lessons.content_html:
Birth and Coming of Age

Jewish family life is shaped by a series of important rituals marking the key stages of life. Brit Milah (circumcision) is performed on the eighth day after a male infant’s birth, fulfilling the sign of the Abrahamic covenant (Genesis 17). Genesis 21:1–8 describes the birth and circumcision of Isaac as the first enactment of this covenant sign. Leviticus 12 sets out the purification rites following childbirth, structuring the community’s response to new life.

Bar Mitzvah (for boys at 13) and Bat Mitzvah (for girls, typically at 12 in Orthodox communities and 13 in Reform) mark the point at which a young person becomes responsible for keeping the Mitzvot. The young person reads from the Torah scroll during a synagogue service for the first time, demonstrating their readiness to fulfil this responsibility. This is one of the most significant events in Jewish family life.

Marriage and Mourning

Jewish marriage is a covenant relationship and a joyful religious celebration. The ceremony includes the exchange of rings, the signing of a ketubah (marriage contract), and the recitation of blessings under a chuppah (wedding canopy). Breaking a glass at the end recalls the destruction of the Temple and expresses that even joy is tempered by remembrance of loss.

Jewish mourning rituals are distinctive and compassionate. Immediately after death, the community organises the tahara (ritual washing of the body) and rapid burial. Shiva lasts seven days: the immediate family stays at home, receives visitors, and is cared for by the community. Avelut covers the broader 30-day period and then the first year. Yahrzeit is the annual anniversary of death, marked by lighting a memorial candle and reciting the Kaddish prayer.

Key Fact

Jewish mourning proceeds in stages: shiva (seven days, family at home receiving community support), avelut (30 days then first year, gradual return to normal life), yahrzeit (annual memorial, candle + Kaddish). These practices reflect the Jewish community’s collective responsibility to support the bereaved, balancing honest grief with eventual return to life.

Shabbat

Shabbat is the weekly day of rest, observed from sunset Friday to nightfall Saturday. Exodus 31:12–18 describes the Almighty commanding Shabbat as the sign of the covenant between the Almighty and the Jewish people: “The Israelites are to observe the Sabbath, celebrating it for the generations to come as a lasting covenant.” The family lights Shabbat candles at sunset, recites blessings over wine (kiddush) and bread (challah), attends synagogue, rests from work and spends time with family and community. Orthodox Jews observe a strict prohibition on all work including using electricity; Reform Jews may observe Shabbat with more flexibility.

Jewish Festivals

Leviticus 23 provides the calendar of the major Jewish festivals commanded by the Almighty:

Rosh Hashanah (New Year, Leviticus 23) is observed in autumn with prayer, the blowing of the shofar (ram’s horn) and reflection on the past year. Yom Kippur (Day of Atonement) follows ten days later — the holiest day of the year, marked by a 25-hour fast, extensive prayer and repentance. Together Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur are known as the High Holy Days.

Pesach (Passover) commemorates the Exodus from Egypt — the Seder meal, with its symbolic foods and retelling of the Exodus story, is the most widely observed Jewish ritual. Shavuot (50 days after Pesach) celebrates the giving of the Torah at Sinai. Sukkot (Tabernacles) commemorates 40 years in the desert by building temporary shelters (sukkot).

Orthodox Judaism observes Shabbat and all festivals strictly according to halakha (Jewish law). Reform Judaism may observe the spirit of Shabbat and festivals while allowing modern adaptations (e.g. driving to synagogue, using electricity). Liberal Judaism is generally more flexible than Reform, often combining traditional forms with a strong emphasis on contemporary relevance. These differences are important for the 12-mark Discuss question, as they show that Jewish practice is not monolithic.

Features of the Synagogue

Synagogue design reflects Jewish beliefs and the importance of Torah. Proverbs 14:28 states: “A large population is a king’s glory” — applied to the synagogue, it affirms the importance of communal gathering. Key features: the Ark (Aron Kodesh) holds the Torah scrolls and faces Jerusalem; the bimah is the raised reading platform; the yad (pointer) is used to follow the Torah text without touching the scroll; the ner tamid (eternal light) burns constantly above the Ark, symbolising the eternal presence of the Almighty. Exodus 27:20–21 commands the maintaining of a perpetual lamp before the Almighty — the biblical basis for the ner tamid.

Key Fact

Synagogue features: Ark (houses Torah scrolls, faces Jerusalem), bimah (raised reading platform), yad (Torah pointer), ner tamid (eternal light — Exodus 27:20–21), menorah (seven-branched lampstand recalling the Temple). Orthodox synagogues have separate seating for men and women; Reform and Liberal synagogues seat families together. These differences in layout reflect theological differences about the role of women in worship.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For the 5-mark question, named sources include Genesis 21:1–8 (birth/Brit Milah), Leviticus 12 (childbirth rites), Exodus 31:12–18 (Shabbat covenant), Leviticus 23 (festivals), Proverbs 14:28 (synagogue community) and Exodus 27:20–21 (ner tamid). Name one specifically. For the 12-mark Discuss, questions about the importance of festivals often ask whether Shabbat or one of the major festivals is ‘most important’ — develop both sides with Exodus 31:12–18 for Shabbat and Leviticus 23 for festivals. The most common error is treating all Jewish communities identically — always acknowledge Orthodox vs Reform vs Liberal differences. SPaG rewards correct spelling of ‘Shabbat’, ‘Rosh Hashanah’, ‘yahrzeit’ and ‘bimah’.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Jewish life-cycle rituals: Brit Milah (Genesis 21:1–8), Bar/Bat Mitzvah, marriage and mourning (shiva, avelut, yahrzeit). Shabbat (Exodus 31:12–18) is observed weekly from sunset Friday to nightfall Saturday as a sign of the covenant.
  • Major festivals (Leviticus 23): Rosh Hashanah (New Year), Yom Kippur (Day of Atonement, fasting), Pesach (Passover/Exodus), Shavuot (Torah at Sinai), Sukkot (40 years in the desert). Orthodox, Reform and Liberal Jews differ in their observance.
  • Synagogue features: Ark (Torah, faces Jerusalem), bimah (reading platform), yad (pointer), ner tamid (eternal light — Exodus 27:20–21), menorah. Seating arrangements differ between Orthodox and Reform/Liberal.

practice_questions.text: Outline three features of a Jewish synagogue and their significance.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for three features with brief significance. Acceptable: Ark (Aron Kodesh) — houses the Torah scrolls and faces Jerusalem, symbolising the direction of prayer; bimah (raised reading platform) — where the Torah is read publicly; yad (pointer) — used to follow Torah text without touching scroll, preserving its sanctity; ner tamid (eternal light) — burns continuously above the Ark (Exodus 27:20-21), symbolising the eternal presence of the Almighty; menorah (seven-branched lampstand) — recalls the Temple in Jerusalem.

practice_questions.text: Describe the Jewish mourning rituals of shiva, avelut and yahrzeit.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each. Shiva: seven-day mourning period in which the immediate family stays at home receiving visitors and community support. Avelut: the extended 30-day period (and first year) of gradually returning to normal life while continuing mourning practices. Yahrzeit: the annual anniversary of death, marked by lighting a memorial candle and reciting the Kaddish prayer.

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which Shabbat is important for Jewish families today.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks per way. Way 1: Shabbat is the weekly covenant sign between the Almighty and the Jewish people (Exodus 31:12-18) — observing it strengthens Jewish identity and reminds families of their special relationship with the Almighty; the Friday evening candle lighting and kiddush create a weekly rhythm of sacred time in the home. Way 2: Shabbat is a time for family togetherness, synagogue community and rest from the pressures of work — in a busy modern world it creates dedicated space for what matters most; it models the Creation narrative where even the Almighty rested on the seventh day.

practice_questions.text:
Explain two ways in which Jewish festivals help Jews to remember the Almighty's actions in history.
In your answer, include a reference to a source of wisdom and authority.
practice_questions.marks: 2 + 2 marks + 1 for named source. Festival 1: Pesach (Passover) commemorates the Exodus from Egypt through the Seder meal, which retells the story of liberation from slavery — this annual re-enactment keeps the formative event of Jewish identity alive for each generation. Festival 2: Shavuot commemorates the giving of the Torah at Sinai — celebrating the moment the Almighty established the covenant relationship with the Jewish people through the Decalogue. 5th mark: ‘Leviticus 23 commands the celebration of these festivals as divinely ordained, ensuring the Jewish community re-enacts its sacred history annually.’

practice_questions.text:
'Shabbat is the most important practice in Judaism.'
Discuss this statement.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (10-12): Both sides developed with named sources; justified conclusion. Arguments in support: Shabbat is commanded in the Decalogue (Exodus 20) — one of the Ten Commandments; Exodus 31:12-18 calls it the sign of the covenant for all generations; it is observed every week, giving it greater frequency than any festival; Rabbi Heschel called Shabbat a 'cathedral in time'; the Talmud treats Shabbat observance as a test case for overall Torah commitment. Arguments against: Yom Kippur is described as the holiest day of the year — its intense focus on atonement and the forgiveness of sins is theologically profound; Pesach commemorates the foundational event of Jewish history (the Exodus); the Shema and Amidah (recited daily) may have a stronger claim on daily Jewish identity than weekly Shabbat; different Jewish communities emphasise different practices. Secure (7-9): Both sides; at least Exodus 31:12-18 named. Developing (4-6): One-sided. Emerging (1-3): Brief.

practice_questions.text: Outline three features of Bar or Bat Mitzvah and why they are important.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each. Acceptable: the young person reads from the Torah scroll in the synagogue for the first time, marking their readiness to fulfil the Mitzvot; the ceremony marks the transition to religious adulthood (13 for boys, 12/13 for girls); the family and community celebrate together, strengthening Jewish identity; the young person delivers a speech ('drasha') on the Torah portion; the Bat Mitzvah is less elaborate in Orthodox communities but equally significant in Reform/Liberal communities.
